subtitle: An independent review of how the website performs for a first-time, full-fee patient — what it does well, and where attention is lost before a consultation is booked.
summary: Two things here are done better than most. “Request a Consultation” is a real, prominent booking action rather than a browse link, and a sticky “Call Now” bar follows the visitor down the page on mobile. That second one is rare and genuinely valuable — a patient who decides halfway down never has to hunt for a way to act.

The opportunity is that the first screen argues instead of proving. “The best med spa in Boca Raton” and “where luxury meets professional excellence” are claims a visitor cannot check, and neither a practitioner nor a patient review appears before the decision point. The evidence that would settle it is stronger than the adjectives currently standing in for it.

Evidence limitation: this review covers the homepage on mobile plus publicly visible information. Treatment-page depth and technical performance were not assessed, so the score is normalised across the six categories that were. Nothing here uses private analytics, and no traffic or revenue figures have been estimated.
scoreNote: Normalised across six assessed categories (90 points available). Treatment content and technical performance were not reviewed and are excluded rather than guessed. The conversion mechanics here are among the better ones we have reviewed — most of what follows is about replacing claims with proof.

scorecard.finding: A superlative claim occupies the space that evidence should hold.
No practitioner, credential or review appears before the decision.
A prominent consultation CTA plus a sticky Call Now bar.
One clear action — with nothing reassuring beside it.
Well built; wide-tracked capitals are harder to read than they need to be.
Boca Raton named in the headline itself.

strengthsLead: The conversion mechanics here are genuinely good. Most of what follows is about what sits around them.

strengths.title: A sticky “Call Now” bar follows the visitor.
strengths.body: Fixed to the bottom of the mobile screen, so a patient who decides at any point can act immediately. Very few practices we review have this, and it is one of the highest-return elements a mobile site can carry.

strengths.title: The call to action asks for a consultation.
strengths.body: “Request a Consultation” names the next step and sits in a large, clearly styled button. Many sites offer “Our Services” in that position and lose the visitor who had already decided.

strengths.title: The location is in the headline.
strengths.body: “in Boca Raton” appears in the largest text on the page — exactly what a patient searching locally needs to see first.

strengths.title: Services are organised by area of concern.
strengths.body: “Face” and the categories beside it match how a patient thinks about the decision, rather than how a clinic files its equipment.

captionDesktop: Desktop, 1366×768. The phone number sits in the header as a button, and Reviews and Gift Cards are both in the navigation — all three good signs. The headline is the superlative claim.
captionMobile: Mobile, 390×844. “The best med spa in Boca Raton”, a prominent consultation button, and a sticky Call Now bar at the foot of the screen.

findings.heading: The headline makes a claim the visitor cannot check.
findings.evidence: The hero reads “THE BEST MED SPA IN BOCA RATON”, with the supporting line “WHERE LUXURY MEETS PROFESSIONAL EXCELLENCE”.
findings.why: A sceptical first-time patient discounts what a practice says about itself, and every competitor claims a version of the same thing. Superlative claims in medical advertising are also an area where the rules vary by state and warrant professional review — that is a question for your own adviser rather than something this review can settle.
findings.recommended: Replace the claim with the proof. A line naming the treating practitioner and their qualification, or a rating with a review count, does more work in ten words than any superlative and cannot be argued with.

findings.heading: No practitioner and no reviews appear before the decision.
findings.evidence: No clinician is named, no qualification or supervising physician is stated, and no patient review or rating appears on the first screen.
findings.why: For injectables the deciding question is who performs the treatment and what they are qualified to do. A patient who cannot answer that here will answer it at a practice that says so plainly — and “the best in Boca Raton” is precisely the kind of claim that makes an unanswered credential question louder.
findings.recommended: Name the treating practitioner with qualification and a real photograph in the hero, and place a rating with its review count beside the consultation button.

findings.heading: The supporting line is set in wide-tracked capitals.
findings.evidence: “WHERE LUXURY MEETS PROFESSIONAL EXCELLENCE” is set entirely in capitals with generous letter-spacing, as are several headings further down.
findings.why: Capitals with wide tracking read more slowly than ordinary sentence case, because the eye loses the word shapes it uses to read quickly. It looks elegant and costs comprehension, which matters most in the line that has to do the persuading.
findings.recommended: Keep the capitals for short labels, and set the sentences that carry meaning in ordinary case.

findings.heading: Nothing reassuring sits beside the button.
findings.evidence: The consultation button stands alone. No review, rating, credential or guarantee appears next to it.
findings.why: The moment a visitor considers pressing a button is the moment doubt arrives. Proof placed anywhere else on the page reaches only the people who were already convinced.
findings.recommended: Put one short patient quote and the review count directly under the button. If the practice holds a strong Google rating, that single line will do more than the headline above it.

psychology.plain: People expect a site to behave like the others they use.
psychology.site: Conventions are followed well. Nothing here surprises or confuses a visitor.

psychology.plain: Important actions should be big and easy to thumb.
psychology.site: Excellent. A large consultation button plus a sticky Call Now bar within thumb reach at all times.

psychology.plain: Reassurance has to sit where the doubt is.
psychology.site: No proof of any kind appears near the consultation button.
No clinician is named on the first screen; the claim of excellence stands unsupported.
Strong — request a consultation, or call. Two routes to the same outcome, both unmistakable.

psychology.plain: Sensible pre-selections that serve the patient.
psychology.site: Organising services by area of concern is a genuinely helpful default for someone who does not know treatment names.

psychology.plain: Balanced, realistic communication is trusted more than perfection.
psychology.site: “The best” is the least believable claim available. Naming what the practice is genuinely best at would persuade more than claiming to be best at everything.

roadmap.actions: Replace the superlative headline with the practitioner's name and credential. Add a rating and review count beneath the consultation button. Set the supporting line in ordinary case.
Practitioner photograph and qualification in the hero. Two patient quotes near the booking action. Treatment-specific reassurance on the highest-value pages.
Treatment-page depth with realistic expectations. Post-treatment review requests to build the rating count. Begin measuring enquiry-to-booking so the calculator figures above become yours.

limitations: This review assessed the homepage at 390 pixels wide together with publicly visible information. Treatment-page depth and technical performance were not assessed and are excluded from the score rather than estimated; the total is normalised across the six categories reviewed (90 points available). Nothing in this report constitutes advertising, regulatory or legal advice.
